TESTIMONY BEFORE THE JOINT STANDING COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE, CONSERVATION AND FORESTRY
in SUPPORT of
"LD606 Resolve, to Study Barriers to Financial Assistance Programs for Farmers and Food
Producers"
Good morning Senator Talbot-Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of Joint Standing
Committee On Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, my name is Annie Watson and I, along
with Heath Miller, represent Maine Dairy Industry Association. (MDIA)
MDIA represents the 138 cow-dairy farms in the state shipping milk. Our farms are located in 15 of Maine's 16 counties. MDIA represents all of Maine's dairies, no matter the size or style of
operation. It is on behalf of these farms that we would like to testify in support of LD606.
There are few of us, working in agriculture, who are necessarily excited about the prospect of
needing financial assistance to support our farm businesses. The stark reality of our food system,
especially in the dairy industry, however, is that revenues received for our food products are
often falling below our costs of production, leaving our farms without means to reinvest into the sustainability of the venture. It is because of this that many of our farms have turned to Federal
and State Programs for financial assistance, especially to allow for investments in much needed
infrastructure updates.
There are valuable opportunities for financial support from both state and federal programs,
however, we consistently hear from our fellow farmers that the challenge of finding and applying
for programs to suit each farm's unique situation and needs can be too complicated or confusing
to navigate. LD606 is a step to better understanding what it is about this programming that prohibits farmers from applying and ultimately benefiting their operations. Our hope is that by
passing this Resolve, the resulting report will translate into policies that will help our farming
community better navigate the ever-changing landscape of these programs.
Thank you for your consideration, and I am happy to answer any questions.

 Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry, thank you for the opportunity
to present to you LD 606, a "Resolve, to Study Barriers to Financial Assistance Programs for Farmers and Food Producers." I am Bill Pluecker and I represent House District 44, constituting the towns of Warren, Hope, and Union.  The premise of this bill came to me as I participated in multiple meetings this past fall with farmers as we discussed the difficulty in finding, applying for, and jumping through bureaucratic hoops to win access to various farmer support programs at the federal, regional, and state level. In one Dairy Task Force meeting that I attended digitally, the idea for having a central list of the various programs was brought up. The farmer mentioned that it was a full time job to research these programs just to determine if the farm would qualify for the program. This does not include the time it would take to apply to the program. Even after finding the program and applying it is still a roll of the dice to see if any funding will come to the farm.  I also spoke with farmers that were new to the industry and did not have the connections either to the Department or the federal offices to know what programming was available, nor the resources to find the information needed to apply to the programs. We all know that we are losing farms and acreage in Maine, and that the only way to stop the hemorrhaging is to increase the number of farms. These programs exist to support these farmers, and creating the connection between the program administrator and the farmers is the first necessary step in supporting them.
As a committee, we heard testimony yesterday from the new Director of the Maine Office of Community Affairs, Samantha Horn, about her own efforts to create a common application for towns and cities in order to access the myriad of programs being offered to towns for development support. Creating a common application for farmers would result in similar synergies as she mentioned yesterday: reduced burden on the applicant, the ability to coordinate applications so the farm receives coordinated support, and the

District 44: Hope, Union, & Warren

ability to put together a plan for the farmer from different sources that results in greater help.
My vision is that the Department might find a way that the many different staff at the Department who are working on various grant programs can collaborate in a way that reduces the burden on the individual staff. They could work together on applications to connect an applicant with various programs being offered from multiple sources that becomes a greater support for the farm. Similar to what was outlined by Director Horn yesterday, I am hoping that a simple one page application could be submitted by a farm annually that would provide the basic data on the operation. Using this simple application, the staff at the Department could be matchmakers, partnering the application with the programs available to the farm. At that point, the staff could support the applicant in submitting a strong proposal for the grant. Of course, nothing would be mandatory, but if a farmer needed support in determining what programs were available and applying for them, they could participate.
I have worked with the Department in order to reduce this bill's burden on staff, reducing the required meetings and listening sessions, and adding the language, "within existing resources." I will continue to work with the Department to ensure that it does not become a burden on them . The bill lays out a framework where the Department will deliver a report about possible points where staff can collaborate internally on programming to increase access to programming for farmers, and externally with other organizations. In January, after the report is delivered, we can come together as a committee to see if there are additional ways that we can offer support to the Department in their effort to reduce barriers and increase access to their programs.
Simplified applications and increased outreach would support new farmers who do not yet have the knowledge of what programming is available and need support in navigating the labyrinth of bureaucracies offering support. This bill would also support established farmers for whom every hour out of the fields and on the computer, is an hour away from the real work of the farm. In light of the likely end to many of the federal dollars and programs on which farmers currently depend, coordinating our remaining resources in order to best serve farmers is more important than ever.
Thank you and I am happy to answer any questions.

IN SUPPORT - LD 606 Resolve, to Study Barriers to Financial Assistance Programs for Farmers and Food Producers
Dear Senator Talbot Ross - Chair, Representative Pluecker - Chair, and members of the Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry,
My name is Christine Cummings and I am the Executive Director of the Maine Grocers & Food Producers Association (MGFPA). The Maine Grocers & Food Producers Association is a business trade association representing Maine's food community; Main Street businesses, including independently owned and operated grocery stores and supermarkets, food and beverage producers and processors, manufacturers, wholesalers, distributors, and supportive service companies.
Maine's food producers and farmers have a significant economic impact here in Maine; Maine's total direct economic impact across agriculture, manufacturing, wholesaling, and on and off-premise retailing creates more than 109,000 jobs, $4B in wages and $15B in output.1 Maine's food producers and farmers are the backbone of our local economy and food system. However, they often face significant financial hurdles, including access to capital, grant funding, and investment opportunities that would allow them to grow and thrive.
We strongly support this proposal to better understand the barriers to accessing financial assistance. As an industry representative, I regularly receive a wide range of communications, including grant opportunities, training and technical assistance programs/webinars/events, and other valuable resources. However, even in an administrative role, managing and disseminating this information effectively can be challenging. While we do our best to share opportunities and stay connected with colleagues and peers, a deeper evaluation of how to streamline financial communication, potentially establishing a central resource hub, and implementing best practices for outreach would ensure that financial opportunities reach the widest possible audience and encourage greater participation amongst Maine's farmers and food producers.
We regularly hear similar feedback that grant applications are time consuming, can be challenging to understand (especially federal grants), and can be very time consuming without resulting in a return on investment if the applicants are not selected as an awardee. Hosting two stakeholder meetings focused on improving access to financial opportunities for food producers and farmers would be a welcomed next step in understanding the challenges and needs of Maine's agricultural community and ensuring that financial resources are accessible, equitable, and effective in supporting longterm success.
We appreciate the steps the ME DACF is taking to improve its current processes and explore potential rulemaking to modernize financial programs. Additionally, expanding the study could provide a more comprehensive understanding of various food-industry organizations, their missions, and projects. This would also help map out key resources, advocates, and financial assistance partners to create a clearer picture of the support landscape.
We look forward to the continued learnings and are willing to assist in connecting our members and colleagues, and ask the Committee to please support LD 606. Thank you for the opportunity to provide testimony.
Christine Cummings Executive Director

Testimony before the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry By Eliza Paterson, American Farmland Trust, Senior New England Policy Associate March 13, 2025
 RE: Support for LD 606 - Resolve, to Study Barriers to Financial Assistance Programs for Farmers and Food Producers  Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry, thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony in support of LD 606.
My name is Eliza Paterson, and I am American Farmland Trust's (AFT's) Senior New England Policy Associate. AFT is the nation's leading conservation organization dedicated to protecting farmland, promoting sound farming practices, and keeping farmers on the land. Since its founding in 1980 by farmers and citizens concerned about the rapid loss of farmland to development, AFT has helped protect over 6.5 million acres of farmland and has led the way for the adoption of conservation practices on millions more. Established in 1985, AFT's New England Program works to save the land that sustains us across the region. AFT has a long history of working in Maine, stemming back to our role in supporting the first farmland protection projects undertaken through the Land for Maine's Future program.
Maine's farmland plays a vital role in our regional economy and food security. Maine has the most agricultural land of any of the six New England states by far, as well as the largest amount of prime and important farmland. According to AFT's Farms Under Threat: The State of the States, roughly 18,000 acres of Maine's agricultural land were converted to urban development or low-density residential land use between 2001 and 2016. This loss of farmland is enough to generate $10 million in annual revenue. To date, Maine has protected less than five percent of the state's farmland. Additionally, without adequate tools for additional farmland protection efforts in Maine, according to AFT's Farms Under Threat 2040, an estimated 53,400 acres of Maine's farmland will be lost to development in the next 17 years.
The intent of LD 606 is to study financial assistance programs to farmers to determine the barriers to these programs and ultimately identify methods of eliminating said barriers and increasing program effectiveness. This is essential helping to keep Maine's farm businesses viable and its farmers on the land.
Ensuring that Maine's farm businesses are financially sustainable is a means to keeping the land that they farm protected. Protecting farms in Maine provides the state with long term food security, meaning that no matter what disruptions impact the global food system, local food can still be provided to Mainers. While the state's food system is supported by mostly small, familyowned businesses, permanently protected farmland benefits all Maine residents, and all types of farmers - both multi-generational farms and new, first-generation farms. More must be done to address the growing threats to Maine's farmland, including real estate development pressures,

land loss due to a changing climate, and high land prices. It is important to note that protecting local farms does not compete with the demand for land dedicated to housing, as agricultural land is generally located away from areas where housing is needed most.
Farm viability and farmland protection will be critical for the future of Maine's local food system and economy. Maine's farmland directly supports the state's economy with over 7,600 farm businesses, close to 13,700 producers, and 15,600 farm laborers. In 2021, the state's agricultural sector produced $21 billion in direct sales with an overall economic impact of $3.6 billion.1
According to a recent report released by New England Feeding New England titled "A Regional Approach to Food System Resilience," it is estimated that nearly 1 million acres of land will need to be brought back into agricultural production if New England wants to produce thirty percent of the food consumed in our region by 2030. The same report also suggests that most of the farmland in the region is located in Maine and Vermont. Keeping Maine's agricultural producers viable and their farm businesses strong will help to ensure that they land they steward will remain in agricultural production. By passing LD 606, Maine has the opportunity to support a more robust state and regional food system.
As a national and regional leader in farmland protection and farm viability, American Farmland Trust fully supports this legislation and urges this committee to pass it this session. If you have any questions, please feel free to reach out to me at epaterson@farmland.org, or Jim Habana Hafner, AFT's New England Regional Director, at jhafner@farmland.org.
On behalf of AFT, thank you for your time and for the opportunity to submit this testimony in support of LD 606.
With sincere regards, Eliza Paterson Senior New England Policy Associate American Farmland Trust
American Farmland Trust is an agricultural non-profit organization with a mission to save the land that sustains us by protecting farmland, promoting sound farming practices, and keeping farmers on the land. AFT is the only national agricultural organization that approaches its work in this comprehensive, holistic manner. We recognize
the connection between the land, forward-looking farming practices, and the farmers who do the work.

LD 606 Resolve, to Study Barriers to Financial Assistance Programs for Farmers and Food Producers
Testimony of John R. Harker Mount Vernon Maine March 13th, 2025
To the Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry Committee.
My name is John Harker. I was the Director of the Division of Resource Development (formally the Division of Market and Production Development) (Formally the Division of Production Development) from 1987 to 2014.
I Administered most of the Financial Assistance and Grant Programs for the Department prior to retirement. I also developed and established Legislation and Rules for a number of the grant and loan programs during my tenure (Agricultural Technology Grant Program, Agricultural Marketing Loan Fund, Agricultural Development Grant Program, Maine Farms for the Future Program, Agricultural Irrigation Source Development Program, and Specialty Crop Grant Program). Most of these programs still exist in some form today.
I would favor this bill, but ask that OPEGA do the study, hopefully a politically neutral agency who could ask the hard questions about political influence both at the appointed level and at the Staff level. Influence is always a problem and is the hidden elephant in the room.
Let me tell you as I have seen it, as to what some of the issues are regarding political influence and access to these programs:
1. The political appointees can and have in the past influenced the access to the programs by wanting the administrators to "assist" their political friends. I found this to be the case sometimes regardless of whether it is a Democrat or Republican in office at the time.
2. Political appointees can influence the access to the program by who gets a grant by determining who gets on the grant review and selection committees. By doing

so the Committee members get to score the applications, sometimes doing so to favor who gets the grants.
3. If the grant program was sent to an outside NGO to administer, I saw some of what I considered with favoritism and lax grant administration.
One farmer friend of mine once said "All grant programs develop winners and losers. That should not be the role of government to give my tax dollars to support my competitor. Leave it to the free marketplace to decide".
Perhaps we should also review the role of government in even being in the grant program business at this time in our history.

Testimony of Nancy Smith, CEO of GrowSmart Maine in support of LD 606, Resolve, To Study Barriers To Financial Assistance

March 11, 2025
Senator Talbot-Ross, Representative Pluecker, and honorable Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry,
My name is Nancy Smith, I live in Ellsworth, and I am the CEO of GrowSmart Maine. We are a statewide non-partisan non-profit organization helping communities navigate change in alignment with smart growth. We advocate for comprehensive policies and funding for smart growth practices and outcomes.
As part of this work, we joined other Maine organizations in helping to design and host last October's Economic Equity Summit. This resolve addresses one of the challenges recognized during the event; that accessing financial assistance programs for farmers and food producers may be challenging to the point of becoming barriers to participation.
As co-owner of a family farm for nearly twenty years myself, I invested time in learning to navigate these processes. This takes time away from the work of farming, though it is often necessary for the continued operation of the farm. Through this resolve, the Department can learn from the intended users of these programs, and adjust their processes to ensure programs are fully utilized by all who could make good use of the financial assistance.
This benefits not only the direct beneficiaries, but all Mainers, in that profitable farms keep farmland in production, in turn reducing sprawling growth while providing access to quality local foods for all of us.
GrowSmart Maine is willing to assist the committee in any way that is helpful.

Testimony of Shelley Megquier, Policy & Research Director, Maine Farmland Trust, to the 132""
Legislature's Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry March 13, 2025
Good afternoon Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry. My name is Shelley Megquier and lam the Policy & Research Director at Maine Farmland Trust (MFT). I am providing testimony on behalf of MFT in
support of LD 606 -- Resolve, To Study Barriers to Financial Assistance Programs for Farmers and Food
Producers.
MFT is a member-powered statewide organization that works to protect farmland, support farmers, and
advance the future of farming. Our goals are to keep agricultural lands working and help farmers and
their communities thrive. Since our founding in 1999, MFT has helped to permanently protect farmland
in every county in Maine, amounting to nearly 57,000 acres across 345 farms. Our Farm Network includes more than 550 farms that have participated in MFT's programming either through an agricultural easement or through one of our programs. Our main program areas are Farmland Protection, Farmland Access, Stewardship, Farm Business Planning, PFAS Support, Climate Resilience, and Policy and Research.
LD 606 requires the Department of Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry to complete a study on barriers to the available financial assistance programs for farmers and food producers operated through the Bureau of Agriculture, Food, and Rural Resources. Through hosting at least two listening sessions, the bill proposes that the Department seeks out greater clarity on what is and what isn't working within its suite of programs and identifies methods for eliminating whatever barriers to access are present. This effort is important so that Maine can ensure equitable access to available programs supported through public investment. MFT's understanding from conversations with farmers and producers is that not everyone is equally informed about available resources and many find navigating various grant applications extremely challenging due to limited time, limited familiarity with the process, language
barriers, or for other reasons. Many farmers jokingly say it could be a full-time job just trying to access
available resources for their farm operation. Though these critiques are typically general and not specific to DACF-operated programs, listening sessions would likely yield additional layers of information to further improve reach, efficiency, and efficacy of these important programs.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide testimony in support of LD 606.
